content.reading_plan: This is a technical research article combining a proposed engineering design, mathematical modeling, literature-based validation, cost accounting, and numerical optimization. Its two-column prose is moderately dense, becoming especially concentrated around equations, assumptions, and cost definitions. I will follow the printed section order, usually taking a few paragraphs at a time and slowing down for the thermodynamic and thermoeconomic models. Figures, tables, and equations will be described as paraphrased readings of those elements. Repeated findings will be noted as restatements rather than treated as new claims, while differences in the paper's successive formulations will be retained.

reading_path.location: p. 10453, Summary
reading_path.moves: States the problem, introduces the proposed intervention and scope, and previews numerical findings and a feasibility conclusion.

claims.text: Waste-heat management has a significant role in energy-efficient data-center operation, but research on waste-heat management for two-phase liquid-immersion cooling remains limited.

The proposed hybrid uses immersion-cooling waste heat to heat the feed side of a direct-contact membrane-distillation module; the investigated cooling loads are 0.7–1.5 kW and membrane areas are 5–75 cm².
The maximum thermal and exergy efficiencies are found as 64.5% and 53.7%, respectively.
Daily distilled-water production can reach 6.13 kg at the highest cooling load and membrane area.
Although the hybrid has higher capital and operating costs than stand-alone cooling, its reported 3.72-year payback makes it economically feasible for real applications.
The hybrid's levelized product cost is 2.69–5.33 SGD/h; the abstract places the optimization trade-off at 1.1 kW and membrane areas of 5.12–5.19 cm².

reading_path.meaning: The opening presents the work as a resource-recovery and cost-reduction proposal, not merely a cooling-performance study. These are announced results; the supporting modeling and calculations have not yet been encountered.

reading_path.location: pp. 10453–10454, Introduction, opening through the classification of cooling systems

reading_path.meaning: The proposed application is positioned as an extension of established heat-recovery practice, with an explicit distinction between a prior suggestion and a detailed modeled system. The sustainability framing adds a value-based rationale alongside the energy-cost rationale.

reading_path.location: p. 10454, Introduction, comparison of liquid-cooling approaches
reading_path.moves: Classifies technologies, compares benefits and drawbacks, and narrows the research gap to system-scale immersion cooling.

claims.text: Liquid cooling removes higher heat fluxes than air cooling because the working liquids have better heat-removal performance.

Indirect liquid cooling is more established but has leakage risks and layout-sizing requirements tied to cooling load; direct cooling avoids server- or rack-level liquid piping and is flexible across loads.
Direct methods include jet impingement, spray cooling, and two-phase immersion; they can operate independently or alongside conventional air cooling.
Two-phase immersion provides a more uniform equipment-surface temperature because it uses latent heat transfer.

support.text: The authors direct readers to four works for details of liquid-cooled systems.

reading_path.meaning: The physical proposal is converted into an idealized computational system. These exclusions define what the later performance and feasibility statements include, while Figure 2 shows that optimization depends on the preceding physical and cost calculations.

Equations (5) and (6) add feed- and permeate-pump power to the respective inlet enthalpy rates; Equation (7) adds the server heat rate to the feed's post-pump enthalpy rate to obtain the tank outlet enthalpy rate.
The tank outlet temperature T3 can consequently be found from its enthalpy.

reading_path.meaning: The first modeling step follows the actual flow sequence. Separate fluid correlations preserve the seawater/water distinction, and the tank balance supplies the hot-side temperature needed for the next calculation.

reading_path.moves: Defines evaluation metrics and connects exergy accounting to a sustainability indicator.

claims.text: Equation (20) evaluates cooling COP as server heat removed divided by feed-pump work, and Equation (21) evaluates membrane thermal efficiency as latent heat flux divided by total heat flux.
GOR measures the share of heat input used in vapor transfer, while PR measures produced clean-water flow relative to inlet feed-water flow; higher GOR is desired.

support.text: Equations (22) and (23) express GOR as latent-transfer heat rate divided by server heat input and PR as product-water mass flow divided by stream 1 mass flow.

claims.text: Equation (24), labeled as exergy efficiency, displays latent-transfer heat rate divided by server heat input.
The sustainability index is the ratio of fuel exergy to destroyed exergy; greater fuel-exergy utilization and lower destruction increase this index.

support.text: Equation (25) gives this ratio, and the index is attributed to Rosen and colleagues.
